instructions: Fill a large pot with water and bring it to a boil over high heat. Meanwhile, cut the 2 lb beef shank into 2 inch chunks.
While the water heats, smash the ginger and 5 garlic cloves with the flat of a knife. Cut 3 of the scallions into 2 inch pieces, cut the onion into wedges and cut the tomato into wedges.

Add the beef to the boiling water. Once it comes back to a boil, cook it for 1 minute. Gray foam will rise to the top. Drain the beef in a colander, rinse each piece under the tap, and wipe the pot clean and dry.

Heat the 2 tbsp oil in the same pot over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the onion, ginger and scallion pieces and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onion is soft and browned at the edges.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, until it smells fragrant.
Add the tomato and cook for 2 minutes, stirring, until it starts to soften and break down.
Stir in the 1 tbsp tomato paste and the 1 1/2 tbsp doubanjiang. Cook for 1 minute, stirring, until the paste turns a shade darker and the oil goes red.
Add the beef, the 1/3 cup soy sauce, the 1/3 cup Shaoxing wine and the 2 tsp sugar. Stir for 1 minute so every piece of beef is coated.

Pour in 9 cups water. Add the cinnamon stick, the 2 star anise, the 2 bay leaves, the 1 tsp fennel seeds, the 1 tsp cumin seeds, the 1 tsp coriander seeds and the 1/4 tsp pepper. Bring it to a boil over high heat.
Turn the heat down to low so it barely bubbles. Cover and simmer for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, stirring once in a while, until a chopstick slides into the beef with no push at all.

Lift the beef out into a bowl with a slotted spoon. Pour the broth through a fine sieve into another pot, pressing on the vegetables, and throw out what's in the sieve. That should be about 6 cups. Put the beef back in the broth and keep it hot over low heat. If you'd like to get ahead, make the broth and beef up to 2 days before and keep them in the fridge.
Taste the broth. If it's flat, add a pinch of salt.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil for the noodles. Meanwhile, cut the 4 bok choy in half lengthwise, thinly slice the last 2 scallions and chop 1/4 cup of the cilantro.
Add the bok choy to the boiling water and cook for 1 minute, until it's bright green. Lift it out with tongs onto a plate.
Cook the 1 lb noodles in the same water as the package says, usually 2 to 3 minutes for fresh noodles. Drain them.
Divide the noodles among 4 big bowls. Ladle the hot broth and beef over them, tuck the bok choy in at the side, and scatter the scallions and cilantro on top.
Serve with the chili oil on the side.
method_notes: Both versions blanch beef shank to clean it, fry onion, ginger, garlic and scallion, cook tomato, tomato paste and doubanjiang into the base, then braise the beef with soy sauce and Shaoxing wine until it's tender and serve it over wheat noodles with blanched bok choy. The Woks of Life (the lead) uses a spice sachet of cinnamon, bay, fennel, cumin, coriander and Sichuan pepper, adds dried chilies, and simmers for about 3 hours on the stove. Omnivore's Cookbook adds carrot and daikon, uses star anise and rock sugar, and tops each bowl with stir fried pickled mustard greens. This follows The Woks of Life's ratios for 2 lb of shank with Omnivore's star anise, strains the spices out instead of using a sachet, leaves the dried chilies and Sichuan pepper out of the pot so the broth stays mild, and puts chili oil on the table; the pickled mustard greens are left out as hard to find.
